item.title: How to Navigate the EU AI Act Explorer
item.description:
The EU AI Act can feel like one more thing to track. New updates arrive. You read long documents. You search the internet for answers. Compliance can feel like this:

This article helps you through that process. The most important resource is the EU AI Act Explorer, built by the European Commission. This article uses Article 50 as the example. Article 50 became enforceable on 2 August 2026. See Article 50 Is Now in Force for what that date changed.

item.title: Claude Will Watermark Its Own Output: What Anthropic's Marking Plan Means for You
item.description:
Anthropic published its plan to mark AI-generated content. It signed the EU AI Act’s Article 50(2) Code of Practice as a provider of generative AI models and generative AI systems. This is the Section 1 half of the framework that we signed under Section 2 as a deployer. Providers build the marking infrastructure. Deployers disclose. This document shows what the provider side will put in your hands.

What Anthropic committed to

Anthropic gives four commitments:

item.title: The Science Talk Signs the EU Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content
item.description:
We signed the European Commission’s Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content, under Section 2, as a deployer of generative AI systems. That puts The Science Talk in the same signatory pool as Bulgari, Getty Images, Lenovo, and Lufthansa. Section 1 of the framework counts Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Mistral among its signatories.

Why this, why now

The AI Act’s transparency obligations become legally binding on 2 August 2026. These are the rules that require AI-generated and AI-modified content to be marked and disclosed. The Commission approved the Code of Practice as the sanctioned route to compliance. Independent experts drafted it. The Commission and the AI Board found it sufficient. It gives signatories “a streamlined, predictable and legally certain pathway,” regardless of which national authority ends up supervising them.

item.title: Regulation as a Feature: The Case for AI Transparency
item.description:
Every conversation about the EU AI Act’s transparency rules starts from the same assumption: this is a cost to minimize. Add the disclosure, tick the box, move on. This framing gets the opportunity backwards. AI transparency, done properly, is a genuine competitive advantage for a small AI-using team that competes against operators who treat it as an afterthought.

The obligation, stated plainly

Article 50 of the AI Act requires providers of certain AI systems to state clearly that people interact with AI. It also requires marking of AI-generated or manipulated content, including deepfakes and AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. These duties apply from 2 August 2026. Following the 2026 Digital Omnibus, generative AI systems already on the market before that date get an extended transitional period to 2 December 2026 to comply with the content-marking requirement specifically.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 50 Is Now in Force: What Changed on 2 August 2026
item.description: As of 2 August 2026, Article 50 of the EU AI Act is an enforceable transparency obligation. It is no longer a future requirement. If you publish AI-generated or AI-manipulated content professionally — text, video, audio, or social posts — the disclosure duty now applies to you. This article explains what that means in practice, and what it does not mean.

item.title: EU AI Act Checklist for Small Business: 6 Articles That Matter
item.description: Most SMEs and agencies file the EU AI Act as someone else’s problem. It has more than 180 articles of dense legal text. The text looks written for hyperscalers and regulators, not a five-person creative studio or a research consultancy. That view is wrong. This is a practical EU AI Act checklist for small business. Six articles decide almost everything a small team needs to know. This is the one-page map to them.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 5: AI Practices You're Banned From Using
item.description: The EU AI Act’s Article 5 prohibited AI practices have applied since 2 February 2025. These are not a future deadline. They are live red lines every organization is already bound by. Most small teams have never read Article 5 in full. They assume “prohibited practices” means something distant, such as mass surveillance, social credit systems, or government overreach. Four of the eight bans sit much closer to home, in ordinary HR, marketing, and analytics tooling.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 4: What Creator Agencies and Small Teams Owe
item.description: If you run a solo AI-assisted content operation, EU AI Act compliance depends mostly on your own choices. If you add a freelancer, editor, or contractor to your team, this changes. Article 4’s AI literacy provision covers anyone who deals with the operation and use of AI systems on your behalf. As of 27 July 2026 that provision is lighter than it was, and most coverage of it still describes the old version.

item.title: Recommender Systems: Even EU Regulators Don't Agree Which Law Applies
item.description:
When stakeholders tell a regulator that a rule is unclear, the regulator’s usual instinct is to insist otherwise. The European Commission’s own review of the Digital Services Act names recommender systems as one of the most-cited areas of stakeholder ambiguity. The review does not dispute the confusion. It documents it.

You may build or operate a recommender system in the EU. It could be a “you might also like” feature, a personalized feed, or a ranking algorithm. This admission from the regulator matters more than any single law firm’s reading of the rules.

item.title: EU AI Act Deadlines 2026–2028: The Current Timeline
item.description: The EU AI Act’s original 2 August 2026 deadline for high-risk AI obligations no longer applies. The European Parliament approved a simplification package on 16 June 2026 (423 votes in favor, 57 against, 174 abstentions) that pushed several key dates back, in some cases by well over a year. This guide gives the current, officially confirmed timeline, sourced directly from European Parliament press releases. It points to which date applies to your situation.

item.title: The AI Act Omnibus Delay: Relief or a Trap for Small Teams?
item.description: The headline version of the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI is simple. The EU pushed the high-risk rules back. Stand-alone high-risk systems now have until 2 December 2027. High-risk systems embedded in regulated products have until 2 August 2028. Both dates are later than the original 2 August 2026 date. This headline will cost some small teams a compliance scramble in eighteen months. They will read “delayed” as “cancelled” and stop preparing.

item.title: The EU AI Act: The Complete Guide for Small Teams
item.description:
The EU AI Act has over twenty separate guides on this site. Each guide covers one article, deadline, or obligation. That depth is useful once you know what you are looking for, but it is a poor starting point. This page is the starting point. It shows what applies to you, in what order, with a direct link to the full guide on each piece.

Source note: every date and obligation below comes from the individual guides linked in this post. Each guide cites official EU Parliament or European Commission material. The 2026 Digital Omnibus simplification package shifted some dates. This guide reflects the current confirmed timeline. Check the lastmod date on each linked guide before you rely on it for a compliance deadline.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 62: Free Support SMEs Can Claim
item.description:
People almost always discuss the EU AI Act as a cost: obligations, documentation, fees. Article 62 runs the other way. It obliges Member States and the EU AI Office to give small teams concrete support in meeting the Act. Most SMEs and start-ups have never read it, so they never claim what it offers.

This guide sets out exactly what Article 62 makes available to small operators, and the route to access each measure.

item.title: GPAI Code of Practice: Provider vs. Deployer, Explained
item.description: Does the GPAI Code of Practice apply to you? For most teams that build AI-powered products, the answer is no. The Code is the European Commission’s voluntary compliance tool for providers of general-purpose AI models under the EU AI Act. The Commission published it on 10 July 2025 after input from more than 1,000 stakeholders. It binds model providers, not the teams that build on top of their models. This guide walks through the provider-vs-deployer test, what each of the Code’s three chapters covers, and what a downstream team building on GPT, Claude, or similar models should take from it.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 25: When You Become the AI 'Provider'
item.description:
Most agencies I speak to treat the EU AI Act as someone else’s problem. They use AI tools, so they assume the heavy obligations sit upstream with OpenAI, Anthropic, or whichever vendor built the model. Almost none of them have read Article 25. This clause moves the provider’s entire obligation set onto ordinary businesses through work they do every week.

This is the most overlooked liability transfer in the Act for creative, marketing, consulting, and research agencies. It does not require you to build a model. It requires you to put a logo on something, adjust it, or point it at a new job. These are the exact activities agencies are paid for.

item.title: EU AI Act Compliance Starter Kit: 5 Steps for Small Teams
item.description:
Small teams tend to bounce off the EU AI Act because it looks like a job for a legal department. It is not. Most of the Act does not apply to most tools. The parts that do apply follow a clear order you can work through in an afternoon.

This starter kit walks a small team through five steps, in sequence, using only official Commission sources. Each step tells you whether you can stop or must continue.

item.title: EU AI Act AI System Definition: The Official 7-Element Test
item.description: The EU AI Act only applies to systems that meet the legal definition of an “AI system” in Article 3(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Before anyone can discuss risk categories, prohibited practices, or compliance obligations, one gateway question comes first: does the tool in front of you qualify. This guide explains the European Commission’s official 7-element test. The Commission published the test as Guidelines on the definition of an AI system, reference C(2025) 5053 final, dated 29 July 2025. This guide turns the test into a checklist you can run against your own tools.

item.title: EU AI Act High-Risk Hiring AI: The Annex III Test
item.description:
Recruitment and HR tools are the single most common place agencies and small teams run into EU AI Act high-risk hiring AI status. Annex III of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 names employment AI directly. The classification test is more mechanical than it looks once you know the three questions to ask. This guide walks through the actual 3-step test, using only the AI Act’s own text.

What you need before starting

  • A list of every AI tool that touches recruitment, hiring, or staff management
  • For each tool, whether you built it, customized it, or use it off-the-shelf
  • Basic clarity on whether you are the provider or deployer of each tool

If you are unsure of the provider/deployer distinction, read the GPAI Code of Practice: provider vs deployer guide first. The Annex III test below assumes you already know which role you hold.

item.title: How to Build an EU AI Act AI System Register (Free Template)
item.description:
Most small teams cannot answer a simple question. Which AI tools do we actually use, and who is responsible for each one? This guide builds an AI system register. It is a tracking sheet you can create in a spreadsheet, Notion, or Airtable. It ends with a short self-test for whether you owe an official EU database filing under Article 71 of the EU AI Act.

What you need before starting

  • A spreadsheet, Notion database, or Airtable base — any tool with rows and columns works
  • About 30 minutes of uninterrupted time
  • A rough list of every department or team using AI tools, so you can ask them directly

This guide covers the internal register only. It does not explain how to file an Article 71 EU database entry. Very few readers of this guide need that yet. The self-test below explains why.

item.title: The EU AI Act: Everything Digital Creators Need to Know
item.description:
Most digital creators think the EU AI Act means one thing. Add an “AI-generated” tag to your video and continue. That is not correct. Article 50 has a hard deadline of 2 August 2026, so it gets all the attention. But it is one article inside a larger framework. Creators who prepare only for the label miss the parts that restrict how they can build and use AI tools.

Here is the quick map before the detail.

item.title: AI Adoption Risks Every European SME Should Know About
item.description: Most European SMEs that adopt AI tools right now make the same decision large enterprises made a decade ago with cloud software, and they are about to discover the same consequences. Tool by tool, subscription by subscription, the dependency architecture builds. By the time the regulatory environment catches up, the cost of changing course is already significant. The December 2025 European Parliament study on software and cyber dependencies puts hard numbers on what this looks like at scale. These numbers are worth knowing before your next renewal or sign-up.

item.title: Claude Adoption in European Research: The Infrastructure Gap
item.description: I have watched the conversation about Claude in European research circles for some time now. The discussion almost always centers on product quality. Is it accurate enough, safe enough, capable enough for research use? Rarely does anyone ask the prior question. Even if researchers want Claude, can they actually get it into their working environment? The barrier to Claude adoption in European research institutions is not the product. It is the vendor integration layer, the procurement frameworks, IT policy, and compliance processes that sit between researchers and new tools.

item.title: How to add AI disclosures that comply with the EU AI Act
item.description: The EU AI Act’s transparency obligations under Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026. If you publish AI-generated content professionally, you have specific disclosure duties. These duties go well beyond a footnote in your terms and conditions. The European Commission published draft guidelines that explain what disclosures must look like, where they must appear, and what does not meet the standard. This guide translates those requirements into practical placement guidance for content creators, freelancers, and science communicators.

item.title: EU AI Act Article 4: What AI Literacy Requirements Mean for European Research Institutes
European Research's AI Problem: Implementation, Not Adoption
item.description:
Understanding where an industry stands on AI adoption is useful. Mapping it systematically, with verified sources, structured synthesis, and clear conclusions, is a different skill. This case study documents a deep research sprint on AI integration across European research institutes. It covers the question, the AI-assisted research method, the evidence, and the strategic meaning.

AI integration in European research institutes is accelerating, at least on paper. Institutes approve strategies. They form committees. They issue press releases. But if you ask most researchers and research managers what AI tools they use in their day-to-day work, and how, the honest answer is usually a shrug, a mention of ChatGPT for emails, and a vague sense that the institution is “working on it.”

item.title: Mapping AI Adoption Across European Research Institutes: A Deep Research Case Study
item.description: Understanding where an industry stands on AI adoption is useful. Mapping it systematically, with verified sources, structured synthesis, and actionable conclusions, is a different skill. This case study documents a deep research sprint on AI integration across European research institutes. It covers the question, how the research team investigated it using AI-assisted research tools, what the evidence shows, and what it means strategically. It is also a worked example of what AI-assisted research analysis looks like in practice, as distinct from AI-generated content.
